summary: ASTRA is an experimental prototype for monitoring astronaut health on long missions, when help from Earth is delayed or unavailable. A sensor rig (an ESP32 with a heart-rate sensor and a motion sensor) feeds a local dashboard that runs on the crew's own computer. The dashboard compares each person with their own usual values and shows plain-language notifications with practical advice in three levels of care: look after yourself, tell the crew medical officer, and in an emergency call the crew and mission control at the same time. A radiation page shows NOAA space-weather data and tells the crew to get ready when the Sun becomes active. ASTRA addresses the challenge "Create Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts on Space Missions": it gathers health indicators and helps astronauts evaluate them and act without waiting for Earth. The advice draws on NASA evidence reports and technical briefs; the alert rules are our own and are not NASA thresholds. In the demo, the earlier days are a labelled simulated baseline and today comes from the live sensor. ASTRA is an educational proof of concept, not a medical device.
details:
What it does. ASTRA brings an astronaut's health indicators and the radiation situation into one local dashboard that runs on the crew's own computer. A sensor board (an ESP32 with a heart-rate sensor and a motion sensor) sends a measurement every 2 seconds. The dashboard compares today with the person's own usual values and shows notifications such as: heart rate different from usual, rest at an unusual time, no movement for a long time, weak signal, lost connection and radiation. Each notification explains in plain words what it means and gives practical first steps in three levels of care, because a long mission may have no doctor on board: look after yourself, tell the crew medical officer, and in an emergency call the crew and mission control at the same time, without waiting for a reply. The board's small screen shows the current notification too.

Radiation. A separate page uses NOAA space-weather data and shows five stages (All clear, Watch, Prepare, Build the shelter, Shelter), so the crew knows when to get ready for a solar storm. ASTRA does not predict storms and has no radiation detector; it shows early signs and says so.

How it works. Sensors, ESP32, USB or Wi-Fi, Flask API, SQLite, web dashboard. The alerts come from documented rules, not a hidden model. Every record is labelled live hardware, simulated, self-reported or external, and a missing value is never shown as zero.

Benefits and impact. Astronauts get an understandable view of their own health and a clear rule for when to ask for help, even when Earth is many minutes away.

NASA basis. The advice is shaped by NASA evidence reports and technical briefs (cardiac rhythm, aerobic capacity, exercise, medical operations, radiation protection). NASA publishes no alert thresholds for these sensors, so the thresholds are our own and are not NASA-approved.

Honest limits. In the demo, the earlier days are a labelled simulated baseline and today comes from the live sensor. The sensors have not been validated in microgravity. Blood oxygen is not calculated by the current firmware. ASTRA is an educational proof of concept, not a medical device.

Tools. Python, Flask, SQLite, pytest; HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Chart.js; Arduino C++ for the ESP32; ESP32, MAX30102, ICM-20948, 16x2 LCD, buzzer. Code: https://github.com/astileandragos/astra-nasa-2026-submission

Creativity. ASTRA puts the crew first and Earth second: it treats the communication delay as a design constraint, and it joins health and radiation in one picture.
